text: Fairmont Logistics is a mid-sized shipping company. Over one week, an attacker takes them from a simple internet scan all the way to stealing customer data, and at every single stage, a real, specific control from this course could have caught it. An attack isn't one event — it's a chain, and breaking any single link stops everything after it.

Stage one, reconnaissance: an internet-wide scan finds Fairmont's exposed ports, the exact pattern Lesson 30 taught you to spot in a capture. A tuned firewall and IDS logging that scan, plus a policy exposing only the ports the business actually needs, catches it here for free. Stage two, delivery: a phishing email with a malicious attachment reaches an accounts-payable employee. Email filtering and real security-awareness training are what stop that attachment from ever getting opened.

Stage three, exploitation: the employee enables macros, and malicious code runs — the attack succeeds. Disabling macros by default, plus least-privilege access from role-based authorization, limits the damage even after that. Stage four, installation: a backdoor installs and persists through a reboot. Endpoint detection and routine monitoring are built to flag exactly that kind of new, unrecognized persistence.

Stage five, command and control: the backdoor beacons out on a steady interval, waiting for instructions — the same unfamiliar outbound pattern from the Wireshark lesson. Egress filtering and network monitoring can block or catch it here. Stage six, actions on objectives: customer records get pulled and exfiltrated through that same channel. Encrypting that data at rest and in transit makes it useless to steal, and compliance frameworks like NIST and ISO 27001 govern the breach response that follows.

Every stage that gets through makes the next one easier and the eventual cost higher — blocking the scan costs a firewall rule, cleaning up after exfiltration costs a forensic investigation and legal exposure. Next up, the final lesson of this course: one realistic SOC shift that pulls every chapter together into a single scenario.
